summary:
A Charter essay uses Christopher Nolan's box-office hit "Odyssey" as a jumping-off point to compare today's knowledge workers not to the heroic Odysseus but to Franz Kafka's 1936 sketch "Poseidon," in which the sea god is an overworked, disaffected office bureaucrat doing monotonous calculations at a desk, feeling stuck in his role, repulsed by the idea of transferring departments, and waiting for the world to end so he can finally get a quiet moment.

Yale psychologist Laurie Santos, host of The Happiness Lab, argues Poseidon is not clinically burned out. Burnout requires three components: personal exhaustion, personal ineffectiveness, and depersonalization or pervasive cynicism. Instead Poseidon is "languishing," a "meh" state that is neither depression nor burnout. The piece links this to current worker data points: rising mental health leaves, reports that workplaces feel less joyful, and record-low confidence in employers, plus a sluggish job market that makes people feel trapped.

The article then offers prescriptions. First, savor small delights, because hedonic adaptation dulls the perks and projects that once appealed; Santos suggests naming two things you like about your job, however small, such as coffee breaks with a work friend. Second, managers should help employees craft more meaningful jobs, citing a 2001 study of hospital janitorial staff who added meaning through small acts like rearranging a patient's room decorations or offering tissues to grieving families. A 2024 study found boredom on one task depresses engagement, attention, and performance on later tasks, but that spillover vanished when the boring task was followed by a meaningful one. UNC Chapel Hill's Shimul Melwani recommends building job-crafting questions into one-on-ones: what is draining you, what is energizing you. Third, invest in "time affluence" and real breaks, countering the "time poor" feeling that UCLA's Cassie Holmes says makes people do less.

claims.claim: Nolan's "Odyssey" film reached global box-office sales of $911 million.
One 2017 translation of Kafka's "Poseidon" is only 410 words long.
Burnout's clinical definition has three parts: personal exhaustion, personal ineffectiveness, and depersonalization or pervasive cynicism; Kafka's Poseidon instead fits "languishing."
claims.attribution: Laurie Santos, psychology professor at Yale and host of The Happiness Lab

claims.claim: Workers are increasingly taking mental health leaves, say workplaces have become less joyful, and report record-low confidence in their employers.
claims.stat: new record lows in employer confidence

claims.claim: A 2001 study showed hospital janitorial staff made their roles more meaningful through small actions such as rearranging decorations in patients' rooms or offering tissues to crying families.
Workers who perform a boring task see engagement, attention, and performance decline on subsequent tasks, but the spillover disappears if the boring task is followed by a meaningful one.
claims.attribution: Shimul Melwani, associate professor, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (previously told Charter)

claims.claim: Feeling "time poor" reduces how much people do.
claims.attribution: Cassie Holmes, professor at UCLA Anderson School of Management
